subtitle: Words, learned expectations and context all shape how people understand each other. Explore how, then practice questions and responses that make the meaning clearer for everyone involved.
scope: For staff across DHS. Original practice examples support both personal cultural understanding and practical communication. You may reflect privately and without recording personal details, or use the complete practice path. This is not a language test, an individual IDI assessment or a guide to predicting people from group labels. Required work and reporting responsibilities stay separate from practice. Native American- and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the person or area responsible within ADSA.
introTranscript: People can use the same words and understand a different invitation, intention or relationship. Intercultural communication involves examining those meanings rather than assuming one familiar reading is universal. In this course, Alex and Toni explore an invitation to contribute at a neighborhood reading event. A separate work example explores an offer of help. You can learn from these cases or examine an expectation privately, without sharing a personal story.

intro.heading: Separate the expression from its meaning
intro.body:
The Council of Europe’s educational account of intercultural competence connects understanding oneself and others with communication across cultural difference. It treats learning as more than knowing facts about groups. The original cases here use that idea to examine meanings in everyday exchanges; they do not reproduce the book’s learning activities or establish Minnesota requirements.

Practice organizer Alex invites Toni to bring a short reading to a neighborhood event: “You can share something, only if you want.” Alex means that contributing is genuinely optional. Toni has learned to hear softened invitations as a considerate way of asking for help without issuing an order. Toni begins preparing a reading despite already having other plans.

Both have heard the same words. Alex’s intention and Toni’s interpretation are different, and neither was made explicit in the first exchange. The misunderstanding concerns the force of an invitation, not a lack of vocabulary or a proven group trait.

The first task is to distinguish the expression from the meanings attached to it. Alex did not explicitly say that a contribution was needed. Toni did not explicitly ask whether declining was acceptable. You can understand that gap through an example without making either person foolish or recording an actual experience.

flashcards.back: The words or behavior someone uses; its meaning is not settled by the expression alone.
The meaning a person gives an expression in context.
An idea about what usually signifies respect, care or responsibility, developed through experience.
Relevant circumstances such as the purpose, relationship and practical situation.
A relevant question or explanation that helps distinguish possible meanings.
An honest action informed by the situation and meaning, within real responsibilities.

items.title: Keep the expression visible
items.body: The invitation includes “only if you want.” That phrase matters, but its presence does not prove how Toni understood it. Reading the words alongside the actual context helps identify the uncertainty without pretending that a literal reading has already settled the whole exchange.

items.title: Name an interpretation as an interpretation
items.body: Toni reads the softened invitation as a considerate request for help. Before Toni explains this, Alex does not know that interpretation. Stating it as a possibility keeps inquiry open; stating it as a trait would claim information the exchange cannot provide.

items.title: Shared language can contain different expectations
items.body: The two people do not need different languages for this misunderstanding to occur. A learned meaning of hospitality or obligation can affect how an invitation is read. That is a reason to ask about this exchange, not to assume every familiar phrase will be misunderstood.

tabs.label: Let the words settle everything
tabs.body: Alex assumes the optional wording guarantees an optional interpretation. This overlooks what Toni may have learned about softened requests. The invitation can remain clear to its speaker while the recipient experiences an unstated obligation.

tabs.label: Let a group label settle everything
tabs.body: Alex assigns Toni a cultural category and decides the invitation’s meaning from that label. This replaces inquiry with prediction. A person’s actual reading may be different, and the situation still needs an explanation.

tabs.label: Distinguish the expression and reading
tabs.body: Alex notices the words and asks what Toni understood. This makes room for the specific difference between optional choice and a softened request. The inquiry can clarify the invitation without declaring one person’s background deficient.

check.question: What is established by the original invitation?
check.correct: Alex used optional wording; whether Toni understood the contribution as optional still needs relevant information.
wrong: Toni must have misunderstood because of a language deficit.
The words prove both people understood the same obligation.
A group label can settle Toni’s interpretation.
check.feedbackCorrect: The expression is known, while its interpretation is not automatically established by the wording, a deficit claim or a label.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A difference in meaning does not establish a language deficit. Shared words do not prove shared obligation, and a group label cannot supply Toni’s actual reading. Keep the expression and interpretation separate before reaching those conclusions.

items.text: Alex says only if you want.
Toni hears a considerate request for help.
Whether Alex actually needs a contribution.

lessons.title: Understand the expectation behind your reading
lessons.summary: Describe how two learned expectations shape the practice invitation.
lessons.objective: Describe how two learned expectations shape the practice invitation.
objectives: Describe how two learned expectations shape the practice invitation.
Compare meanings of care without ranking them.
Explain why private cultural self-understanding can matter alongside practical communication.
takeaways: An interpretation can have a meaningful history.
Different expressions can serve a shared value.
Private insight does not need a work outcome.
lessons.statement: Examine why your reading makes sense to you before expecting another person to share it.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Understand the expectation behind your reading
intro.body:
Alex learned to show care by leaving another person free to choose. Explicitly optional language has helped Alex avoid imposing. Toni learned to show care by recognizing a need that a considerate host would not announce as a demand. Preparing the reading seems like a way to respond generously.

These practice accounts explain how the same invitation can be read differently. Neither makes a whole community uniform, and neither proves every softened phrase carries the same meaning. The point is to understand the relation between experience, value and interpretation in this case.

A shared value such as care does not eliminate the difference in expression. Saying “both people are kind” can be true and still leave Toni preparing for an obligation Alex never intended. Examining the actual meanings allows the common value and the practical difference to be visible together.

A learner may privately recognize a similar connection in personal experience: perhaps independence, attentiveness or reciprocity has shaped what feels considerate. That understanding is a legitimate result in its own right. There is no requirement to convert it into a written work improvement or disclose where it came from.

Compare meanings of care without ranking them.
Explain why private cultural self-understanding can matter alongside practical communication.
What can a learner recognize?
lessons.keyStatement: Examine why your reading makes sense to you before expecting another person to share it.

items.title: Find the value in the interpretation
items.body: Toni’s reading is connected to being responsive to a host’s possible need. Alex’s reading is connected to not imposing. Understanding the value makes the difference richer than a mistake in wording; it helps explain why simply repeating the same phrase may not resolve it.

items.title: Keep the difference visible within commonality
items.body: Recognizing care in both accounts can support respect, but it should not erase the different expectations. The task still includes whether a reading is wanted or needed. Shared goodwill is a useful connection rather than an answer to every practical question.

items.title: Allow a personal result
items.body: A private recognition about reciprocity may matter even if the learner never organizes an event. Learning about one’s own cultural meanings is not merely a tool for efficiency. The practice path remains available for anyone who prefers to keep personal reflection separate.

tabs.label: Rank the meanings
tabs.body: A learner decides Alex’s explicit choice is modern and Toni’s attentive obligation is inferior. This turns comparison into a ranking before examining the actual purpose. It can make useful self-understanding harder by replacing inquiry with judgment.

tabs.label: Erase the meanings
tabs.body: A learner says both people care, so no difference needs attention. This preserves commonality but leaves the invitation unresolved. Toni may still prepare unnecessarily while Alex believes a free choice has already been communicated.

tabs.label: Compare without erasing
tabs.body: A learner recognizes care in both accounts and identifies the different expectations of obligation. This supports understanding without forcing a hierarchy. The practical invitation can then be clarified while personal insight remains a worthwhile outcome.

check.question: What is the useful comparison?
check.correct: Alex links care to explicit choice; Toni links care to noticing a softened need, and the practical obligation still needs clarification.
wrong: One meaning is inherently superior because it is familiar.
Shared care means the invitation has no unresolved difference.
A private cultural insight matters only if it improves workplace performance.
check.feedbackCorrect: The comparison preserves the values, their different expressions and the actual question without ranking people or making work application a requirement.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Familiarity is not a basis for ranking meanings. Shared care does not answer whether the reading is needed. Personal insight also has value without a workplace result. Examine the connection between value and expectation while keeping the practical difference visible.

items.text: Alex associates care with leaving a choice open.
Whether the contribution is required remains unclear to Toni.
The unfamiliar meaning must be inferior.
Toni associates care with recognizing a host’s need.
Toni begins preparing while Alex expects a free choice.
Private reflection is useless without a work change.

options: Both values and the different expectations, without making personal insight prove a work result.
Only the value behind the familiar account.
A shared value makes every practical difference irrelevant.
responses: This preserves meaningful comparison and personal learning.
Both accounts deserve examination rather than a familiarity preference.
The invitation still has a practical question.

lessons.transfer: Stay with the practice comparison or consider a learned value silently. You can keep the insight private and choose no later work application.

move.control: You can examine the history of your interpretation without judging your whole identity.
move.failure: A common value erases the difference or an unfamiliar expression is ranked as deficient.
move.next: Name the value, its learned expression and the difference that still matters.

lessons.title: Listen for meaning rather than a familiar answer

objectives: Identify what a volunteered explanation actually adds.
Distinguish listening from forcing an account into a preferred story.
Develop a relevant restatement that leaves room for correction.
takeaways: A volunteered account should change what you consider.
Listening is not the same as collecting a biography.
A restatement can be offered for correction.
lessons.statement: Let the account inform your understanding without deciding more than the person said.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Listen for meaning rather than a familiar answer
intro.body:
Toni tells Alex, “I thought you might need someone to fill a gap, and I did not want you to have to ask directly.” Alex can hear a specific meaning of the invitation. If Alex responds, “So you dislike free choice,” the account has been forced into a story Toni did not provide.

A more accurate restatement is, “You heard this as a way of asking for help without putting pressure on me to say I needed it.” Alex can leave room for Toni to correct that reading. The restatement is useful because it connects the account to the actual exchange, rather than demand a complete cultural history.

Listening also includes the practical question. Alex does not need to keep requesting personal explanations after Toni has clarified enough to make the invitation understandable. An ordinary choice should not depend on satisfying the other person’s curiosity about identity.

The learning is not a trick for making Toni agree. Alex’s purpose is to understand the interpretation and make an honest response. Toni can decline further explanation, and Alex can still clarify whether a contribution is needed.

Distinguish listening from forcing an account into a preferred story.
Develop a relevant restatement that leaves room for correction.
Which response supports listening?
lessons.keyStatement: Let the account inform your understanding without deciding more than the person said.

items.title: Notice what the explanation changes
items.body: Before Toni speaks, Alex may think the optional phrase was simply ignored. The volunteered account offers another interpretation: Toni heard a considerate request. This is a meaningful shift in understanding, not evidence that the person cannot read or choose.

items.title: Use a tentative restatement
items.body: A restatement helps only if Toni can correct it. Declaring “I know exactly how you think” would close the inquiry. Alex can describe the specific interpretation heard and invite correction without asking Toni to validate an entire cultural theory.

items.title: Stop when the relevant purpose is served
items.body: Understanding the invitation does not require learning every experience that shaped Toni. A larger personal account may be volunteered, but it should not become the price of an ordinary choice. The actual event question can be answered without exhaustive disclosure.

tabs.label: Fit the account to your story
tabs.body: Alex hears Toni’s explanation but concludes that Toni dislikes choice. This repeats the listener’s interpretation rather than engage the supplied meaning. The response can sound attentive while leaving the central misunderstanding untouched.

tabs.label: Collect the whole background
tabs.body: Alex asks for every family and community influence before clarifying the invitation. This makes the inquiry larger than its purpose and may pressure disclosure. More personal information is not automatically needed to understand this exchange.

tabs.label: Restate and allow correction
tabs.body: Alex offers a specific reading of Toni’s explanation and leaves room for correction. This makes listening visible without claiming complete knowledge. Alex can then answer the practical question while accepting that some personal meaning remains private.

check.question: Which restatement best fits Toni’s account?
check.correct: You heard the invitation as a considerate way of asking for help; please correct me if that is not what you meant.
wrong: Your whole cultural group never asks directly.
Tell every experience behind this before I clarify the invitation.
check.feedbackCorrect: The restatement follows the supplied account and permits correction without adding a trait, group rule or disclosure requirement.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Disliking choice was not part of Toni’s account. A group-wide rule adds information not supplied, and a complete history is unnecessary for the invitation. Restate the specific meaning tentatively and leave room for correction.

items.text: Toni thought Alex needed help filling a gap.
You heard this as a softened request; is that accurate?
You must dislike making choices.
Toni did not want Alex to have to announce a need directly.
Please correct the meaning I understood.
Describe your entire background before I answer.

options: Treat the explanation as a group-wide rule.
Restate the specific meaning and allow correction.
responses: The explanation belongs to this person and exchange.

lessons.title: Clarify the choice and its context
lessons.summary: Develop a question that clarifies the force of a practice invitation.
lessons.objective: Develop a question that clarifies the force of a practice invitation.
objectives: Develop a question that clarifies the force of a practice invitation.
Distinguish intention, practical need and available choice.
Explain why asking whether a contribution is needed can be more useful than repeating the wording.
takeaways: A relevant question can clarify a real choice.
Intention and practical need are related but different.
Choice should not require a private explanation.
lessons.statement: Clarify what the invitation asks of the person and what is actually possible.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Clarify the choice and its context
intro.body:
Toni can ask, “Would the event be short of a reader if I did not contribute?” This question concerns the actual need. It does not demand that Alex explain an entire history of hospitality. Alex can answer, “We have the planned readings covered. I wanted to offer you a chance, and declining would be fine.”

That response clarifies the difference between an optional opportunity and a request to fill a gap. It also supplies practical context that the original softened invitation did not make explicit. Alex is not merely repeating “only if you want” louder.

If a reader were actually needed, Alex could state that honestly and still accept Toni’s answer. Saying a choice is optional while concealing a known practical expectation would not make the communication respectful. Understanding different invitation meanings should improve clarity about the choice rather than provide a technique for obtaining agreement.

In an actual work setting, some choices are constrained by assigned responsibilities or required procedures. A speaker should state those accurately instead of calling every task optional. The neighborhood fiction concerns a voluntary contribution, not a rule for making every DHS responsibility voluntary.

Distinguish intention, practical need and available choice.
Explain why asking whether a contribution is needed can be more useful than repeating the wording.
How should Alex answer?
lessons.keyStatement: Clarify what the invitation asks of the person and what is actually possible.

items.title: Ask about the relevant consequence
items.body: Toni’s question identifies whether declining would leave an unmet need. It gives Alex a practical point to clarify. Asking “What culture makes you invite this way?” would be less useful and could introduce a group explanation neither person needs.

items.title: Keep intention and arrangement honest
items.body: Alex intended a genuine choice and knows the planned readings are covered. Stating both makes the invitation clearer. If the arrangement were different, the answer should change; culturally informed communication cannot rely on a comforting description that is not true.

items.title: Describe the choice without requiring reasons
items.body: Toni can decline without proving the other plans are worthy. The practical arrangement, not a personal disclosure test, explains why this is the person’s own choice. A work requirement would need its own accurate explanation rather than be imported into the social example.

tabs.label: Repeat the softened wording
tabs.body: Alex repeats the original phrase without clarifying whether help is needed. The words remain familiar to the speaker but the practical ambiguity can persist. Repetition may not answer the meaning Toni is trying to understand.

tabs.label: Conceal the expectation
tabs.body: Alex says the contribution is up to Toni while privately expecting Toni to fill a known gap. This uses polite wording to hide pressure. It may obtain participation but does not make the person’s choice informed.

tabs.label: Clarify need and choice
tabs.body: Alex explains that planned readings are covered and that the invitation was an opportunity. Toni can decide without supplying a personal justification. The clarification respects different learned meanings while making the actual arrangement explicit.

check.question: Which response resolves the practical invitation most directly?
check.correct: The planned readings are covered; I meant to offer a chance, and declining is fine.
wrong: Only if you want, repeated without explaining the need.
It is optional, even though I am secretly relying on your contribution.
You must explain your private plans before I accept a decline.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response states the actual arrangement and intention, making the available choice clear without hidden pressure or disclosure.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Repetition may leave the original question unanswered. Concealing reliance makes the optional description misleading. Requiring private plans turns a free choice into a justification test. Clarify the actual need and accept the choice the situation permits.

items.text: Would the event lack a reader if I declined?
The planned readings are already covered.
I call it optional while secretly relying on your contribution.
Is this an invitation or a request to fill a gap?
You can decline without explaining private plans.
Prove your other plans deserve priority.

options: Explain the actual arrangement and genuine choice.
Hide a different expectation behind polite words.

responses: This makes the invitation interpretable and honest.
Hidden pressure does not resolve the misunderstanding respectfully.
A free choice does not require that disclosure.

lessons.transfer: Use the practice question and response. If reflecting on your own invitations, you can keep that examination silent and decide whether any application is relevant.

move.control: You can state the practical need and choice honestly.
move.failure: Polite wording conceals an expectation or leaves the actual question unanswered.

Distinguish an offer of support from required review.
Retain actual responsibilities while adapting an expression.
takeaways: An offer of help can be read in more than one way.
Clarifying meaning is different from changing a requirement.
An authentic response can stay honest about both.
lessons.statement: Use the relevant meaning to improve the exchange without misrepresenting the work.

intro.heading: Make a suitable response in a work exchange
intro.body:
In a separate practice DHS exchange, mentor Lee says to new colleague Jordan, “I can take another look if you want.” Lee intends an optional offer of support. Jordan hears a suggestion that the work has a problem and feels expected to accept before it can proceed. Jordan volunteers that in previous experience, a senior person’s understated offer often indicated something needed attention.

Lee can clarify the offer’s actual purpose and distinguish it from the work’s real review requirements. For this practice task, the separate required review is already identified; Lee’s additional support does not replace it. Lee can say that the offer is optional and name the kind of help available without falsely certifying that the work is ready.

This is a meaningful adaptation because Jordan’s supplied account changes the response: the offer now states its purpose and relationship to required review. Merely supplying an extra document would not, by itself, demonstrate a culturally informed shift. No exchange here establishes Jordan’s or Lee’s individual orientation on the official five-orientation IDC.

DHS’s actual equity-analysis responsibilities continue to apply to relevant work. Communication learning is one way to make those responsibilities understandable, not an alternative to them. Jordan retains ownership, and program consultation can provide guidance and feedback without becoming a mandatory personal approval gate.

Distinguish an offer of support from required review.
Retain actual responsibilities while adapting an expression.
What should Lee do?
lessons.keyStatement: Use the relevant meaning to improve the exchange without misrepresenting the work.

items.title: Let the account change the response
items.body: Lee now understands that the phrase may sound like a disguised correction rather than a free offer. Clarifying the purpose directly addresses that meaning. This is more specific than changing the format without examining what the offer signifies.

items.title: Name the separate review accurately
items.body: Mentoring that a person can accept or decline and required review are different. Lee should explain the actual relationship without announcing a new rule or promising that the work needs no further examination. This lets Jordan make a choice about support while retaining responsibility for the task.

items.title: Keep the response authentic
items.body: Lee need not imitate Jordan’s previous communication pattern. An honest statement of available help, purpose and limits can bridge the meanings. The response is suitable because it makes the relevant distinction clearer, not because it guarantees agreement or a measured intercultural result.

tabs.label: Declare the recipient oversensitive
tabs.body: Lee dismisses Jordan’s reading as an unreasonable reaction. This misses a supplied meaning that could help clarify the offer. The work may continue with the same confusion about whether support is optional or necessary.

tabs.label: Make every step optional
tabs.body: Lee removes the task’s required review to avoid discomfort. This changes the actual responsibility rather than clarify communication. Respecting a meaning does not authorize the mentor to waive a required process.

tabs.label: Clarify purpose and responsibility
tabs.body: Lee explains the offered support and the separate required review. Jordan can use the offer without mistaking it for hidden correction or final approval. The response changes in light of meaning while staying truthful about the work.

check.question: What makes Lee’s response culturally informed?
check.correct: Jordan’s volunteered meaning changes how Lee explains the offer, while the actual review responsibility remains clear.
wrong: The response automatically places Lee in Adaptation.
Any extra document proves a culturally informed response.
check.feedbackCorrect: The connection is between the supplied meaning and the revised explanation, not a personal assessment, waived duty or format change alone.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A single response cannot establish an individual orientation. Respect does not waive required review, and an extra document need not reflect any perspective shift. The account should inform a suitable truthful response while actual responsibilities remain intact.

items.text: Jordan hears a senior offer as a sign that something needs attention.
Lee explains the offer’s optional purpose.
The offer proves Lee’s individual IDC orientation.
Jordan connects the reading to prior experience.
Lee distinguishes support from the actual required review.
Remove required review solely to avoid discomfort.

responses: The mentor cannot change the duty through this learning exchange.
The account provides useful relevant information.
This connects meaning to a truthful response and a real choice.

move.control: You can explain a support offer without making false assurances.
move.failure: A relevant meaning is dismissed or a responsibility is changed to avoid discomfort.

lessons.summary: Develop a repair that addresses the specific meaning gap.
lessons.objective: Develop a repair that addresses the specific meaning gap.
objectives: Develop a repair that addresses the specific meaning gap.
Distinguish clarification, changed understanding and an unknown effect.
Preserve the formal response when a concern is more than an ordinary misunderstanding.

A formal concern needs its actual response.
lessons.statement: Repair the specific gap and describe what changed without claiming the whole relationship is resolved.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Repair misunderstanding and keep an honest account
intro.body:
Alex discovers that Toni spent time preparing a reading because the invitation was heard as a softened request. A useful repair acknowledges the gap: “I did not make clear that the event was covered and that this was a genuine option.” Alex can clarify the arrangement and ask what Toni now prefers without requiring reassurance.

Toni may still choose to contribute, decline or leave some personal explanation private. Agreement with a particular next step is not proof that every relationship concern has disappeared. Alex can accurately say the invitation’s purpose was clarified; its effect on trust may remain unknown.

An ordinary misunderstanding should not be used to explain away every work concern. Under MMB Policy 1436, managers and supervisors immediately report protected-class allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow their assigned agency procedures. A communication repair neither establishes a violation nor replaces required reporting, non-retaliation or an authorized investigation.

For learning, you can retain a private insight about a phrase or expectation without performing a real repair. For an actual relevant exchange, a suitable repair addresses the specific meaning and any responsibilities that remain. The account of progress should distinguish what was clarified, what the person actually said and what is still unknown.

inThisLesson: Develop a repair that addresses the specific meaning gap.
Distinguish clarification, changed understanding and an unknown effect.
Preserve the formal response when a concern is more than an ordinary misunderstanding.
How should progress be described?
lessons.keyStatement: Repair the specific gap and describe what changed without claiming the whole relationship is resolved.

items.title: Acknowledge the gap without demanding forgiveness
items.body: Alex can name the missing practical explanation and its consequence for preparation. Asking Toni to say the relationship is fine would make the repair serve Alex’s reassurance. A proportionate acknowledgment leaves Toni free to choose what to share or do next.

items.title: Describe a modest result
items.body: The arrangement can be clarified even when trust has not been discussed. Alex should not make a larger claim from a chosen next step. This protects the usefulness of the real clarification without turning a limited result into a story about complete resolution.

items.title: Recognize the separate responsibility
items.body: A protected-class allegation is not handled solely as a style misunderstanding. A manager’s required report and actual assigned process remain. Respectful clarification can support communication, but it cannot be used to delay the response or privately decide the allegation’s merits.

tabs.label: Seek reassurance as the repair
tabs.body: Alex asks Toni to confirm there was no problem. This can pressure the person to minimize the effect of the unclear invitation. It replaces an acknowledgment of the gap with a desired emotional outcome for the speaker.

tabs.label: Claim complete resolution
tabs.body: Alex treats Toni’s chosen next step as proof that all trust is restored. The choice provides information about the activity, not every dimension of the relationship. A larger claim needs its own evidence and should not be inferred automatically.

tabs.label: Repair and keep unknowns visible
tabs.body: Alex acknowledges the missing context, clarifies the choice and accepts Toni’s next step. The practical result can be described accurately while any wider effect remains open. In work, separate formal duties still receive their required response.

check.question: What can Alex accurately say after clarifying the arrangement?
check.correct: The invitation’s purpose and available choice were clarified; any wider effect not discussed remains unknown.
wrong: Toni’s next step proves all trust is restored.
A protected-class allegation becomes optional after an apology.
Private learning failed unless a real repair was performed.
check.feedbackCorrect: A limited clarification can be valuable without proving trust, waiving a formal duty or requiring an actual personal interaction.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A chosen next step does not establish every effect on trust. An apology does not remove required reporting of a protected-class allegation. Private cultural learning can also be worthwhile without a real repair. Describe the specific result and retain separate responsibilities.

items.text: Alex explains that planned readings are covered.
Toni chooses whether to contribute.
The effect on trust has not been discussed.
Alex states the invitation was genuinely optional.
Toni declines further personal explanation.
Whether future invitations will be interpreted differently.

options: State the clarification and chosen response while keeping wider effects unknown.
Require Toni to confirm restored trust.
responses: This gives an accurate account of the limited result.
The evidence does not support that larger claim.
Reassurance should not be the price of the repair.

lessons.transfer: Use the practice repair or keep a private insight about an expectation. No real disclosure, written personal note or work result is required for the learning to matter.

move.control: You can acknowledge the specific gap and keep the result accurate.
move.failure: Repair becomes reassurance, a complete-resolution claim or a substitute for a formal duty.
move.next: Name the gap, clarify the choice and distinguish the response from the unknown effect.

jobAid.subtitle: Examine a message, clarify its meaning and choose an honest response without predicting a person from a label.
remember: Words, intention and interpretation are connected but are not identical.
A learned meaning can be worth understanding privately, without a required work application.
A suitable response retains actual responsibilities and does not establish an individual assessment.

sections.heading: Examine the exchange
items: Identify the words or action, your reading and what remains unknown.
Notice the value or expectation that makes your reading familiar.
Use an original learning example or reflect silently; no personal history needs to be entered.

sections.heading: Clarify the relevant meaning
items: Ask about the actual need or choice rather than require a complete cultural explanation.
Restate a volunteered account tentatively and leave room for correction.
Explain your purpose and any real constraint honestly; do not hide pressure behind optional wording.
Accept that some personal meaning may remain private.

sections.heading: Respond and follow through
items: Let the relevant account change the explanation or action where appropriate.
Keep optional support distinct from the actual review or access responsibilities.
Acknowledge a specific gap without requiring reassurance or forgiveness.
Managers and supervisors immediately report protected-class allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow assigned procedures.
Describe the clarification and actual response separately from a wider effect that has not been checked.

sources.title: Council of Europe: Developing intercultural competence through education
sources.note: Conceptual educational account of self-understanding, perspective-taking and intercultural communication. Original invitation and support cases are newly authored, not copied source exercises or Minnesota procedural requirements.

sources.title: Intercultural Development Inventory: The Intercultural Development Continuum
sources.note: The distinct official five-orientation continuum and culturally informed perspective-and-behavior meaning of Adaptation. A course response or ordinary communication adjustment does not establish an individual orientation.

sources.title: DHS Equity Policy
sources.note: Actual staff equity-analysis responsibilities remain in place. Required analysis still applies, and staff keep ownership of their work.

sources.title: MMB Policy 1436: Harassment and discrimination prohibited
sources.note: Immediate manager and supervisor reporting, actual assigned procedures and non-retaliation are distinct from ordinary misunderstanding, clarification and apology.
